findings.title: `--here` with a PATH that has `..` in it searches nothing on Linux and macOS (a linked folder inside a search location fails the same way)
findings.scenario: Home is the search location. In ~/src/app run `fffinder ../lib --query parser --here` (or `fffinder .. --here` and type a word; the same when a running copy takes the launch, and with `--pick`). The window opens the right folder and lists its items, Search Only in "lib" is on, and the search says No Results although files in the folder match. Without `--here` the same words find them, and `cd ../lib; fffinder --here --query parser` works, because the shell's folder comes without `..`. Expected: the folder's matches, as the manual says of `--here`. Windows is not affected: std::path::absolute resolves `..` there, while on POSIX it keeps it. The root cause is older than the branch (the toolbar's Search Only in button fails the same way in a window opened with `fffinder ..`), but `--here` is the branch's documented way to get there in one command. Same outcome for a PATH that is a symlink inside a search location (follow_symlinks is off by default, so the index has nothing under the link's name).
findings.code_path: src/lib.rs:44-45 and 336-341 (start_location: std::path::absolute keeps `..`, the result becomes Location::Folder); src/lib.rs:54-57 (the same path is handed to a running copy); src/lib.rs:148-155 and src/finder/mod.rs:1181-1194 (open_request navigates to it, then search_here); src/finder/mod.rs:2157-2162 and 2194-2205 (the scope of the search is current_folder() as spelled); crates/fffinder-core/src/engine.rs:818-822 (root_spelling returns None because `/home/u/src/app/../lib` starts with the root as text, so nothing is canonicalized); engine.rs:134-140 and 1058-1065 (in_base keeps `app/../lib`, folder_glob at 2756-2769 writes it as the glob `app/../lib/**`, which no indexed path matches); engine.rs:1112-1118 (in_scope: path.starts_with(scope) is false for every hit). The contents search does the same at engine.rs:1394-1400 and 1517-1521.
findings.tests_gap: Every test hands open_request, start_location and the second launch a clean absolute fixture path (tests/finder.rs a_search_sent_with_here_stays_in_the_folder, here_is_the_folder_the_window_goes_to, a_window_opened_with_here_shows_nothing_from_outside_its_folder; tests/server.rs a_second_launch_hands_here_to_the_running_window passes fx.tree()). The real-app runs in the record used `Projects`. The Nushell tests go through `path expand`, which resolves `..`, so `fff gui` and `fff pick` are not affected and hide it.
findings.fix: Clean the folder where it comes in: in start_location (src/lib.rs:338), for the hand-off path (src/lib.rs:56) and in Finder::open_request, use the folder's real spelling when it exists (std::fs::canonicalize on Unix, std::path::absolute elsewhere). The shell's folder already arrives that way. Alternatively in the engine: have root_spelling canonicalize also when the scope starts with a root as text and return the respelled path when it differs, and use the same path in indexes_for.
findings.test_idea: In crates/fffinder-core/src/engine.rs, searches_a_folder: add a search for `readme` with scope Some(dir.join("docs/notes/..")) and expect 1 hit; today 0. In tests/finder.rs: open_request(Some(&fx.path("Projects/atlas/..")), Some("atlas"), true, ..) and expect Project Atlas.txt among ui.names(); today the list is empty. A unit test in src/lib.rs: start_location(Some(&dir.join("a/..")), &config) is Location::Folder(dir).

findings.title: A folder spelled in another letter case is searched as spelled: `--here` finds nothing on macOS and Windows
findings.scenario: macOS, home is the search location, the folder on disk is ~/Documents: `fffinder ~/documents --query report --here`. The window lists the folder (the file system ignores case), Search Only in "documents" is on, and the search says No Results. Windows, in PowerShell, which keeps a folder's name as typed: from C:\Users\me run `cd documents`, then `fffinder --here --query report`: the same. Also `"in_folder": true` in POST /v1/open and `scope` in /v1/find with such a spelling; `fff find --here` and `fff search --here` send $env.PWD as it is. Expected: the folder's matches. Only a spelling that differs inside the search location fails: when the search-location part itself differs (`/users/me/Documents`), root_spelling canonicalizes and the search works. As with the `..` finding the weakness is older than the branch (the Search Only in button after Go to Folder with a lowercase path), and `--here` adds the command-line way into it. By reading only; nothing was run on macOS or Windows.
findings.code_path: src/lib.rs:44 (shell_folder: std::env::current_dir, which on Windows is the string the shell set), src/lib.rs:336-341 (std::path::absolute keeps the typed case); src/finder/mod.rs:2157-2162 (scope = current_folder()); crates/fffinder-core/src/engine.rs:818-822 (root_spelling: `/Users/me/documents`.starts_with(`/Users/me`) is true, so it returns None before canonicalizing); engine.rs:134-140 (in_base keeps the typed rest); engine.rs:1061-1065 (glob `documents/**`, matched letter for letter: fff-search-0.11.0/src/index/constraints.rs compile_one builds a case-sensitive globset::Glob); engine.rs:1112-1118 (in_scope compares path components exactly, so nothing under `Documents` is in scope).
findings.tests_gap: Nothing ran on macOS or Windows, and every fixture uses one spelling of its folders. On Linux a folder in another letter case doesn't exist, so no test there can show it. The symlink respelling that root_spelling does is tested (protocol.md's /private/var case); the case inside a root is not.
findings.fix: The same place as the `..` finding: take the folder's on-disk spelling when it comes in. In the engine, the smallest change is in root_spelling (engine.rs:818-832): drop the early return, canonicalize the scope, and return the root-spelled path (r.path joined with the rest after r.canonical) whenever it differs from what was given; the recursion in search and grep_cancellable ends because the second call gets the path it would return.
findings.test_idea: An engine test for macOS and Windows only (#[cfg(any(target_os = "macos", windows))]): a root with Docs/readme.md, search `readme` with scope root.join("docs"), expect readme.md; today nothing. To have one that fails on Linux too, take the respelling out into a function that is given the canonical path (respell(scope, canonical, roots)) and test that `/r/docs` with canonical `/r/Docs` comes back as `/r/Docs`.

findings.title: Searching one large folder for a word that is in the folder's own path loses real matches: fff-search fills the pool with matches the engine then discards
findings.scenario:
Steps: a search location /data; the folder /data/work holds more than about 4,000 items; turn on Search Only in "work" and type `work`. Same shape: `photo` in Photos, `doc` in Documents, `contoso` in `OneDrive - Contoso`.

What happens: the folder reaches fff-search as a glob constraint, which narrows the files but not the text matched. fff-search still matches the word against each item's path from the search location down, and that path begins with `work/`. Every item in the folder is therefore a match with one score: 60 for `work` (4 x 12, plus frizbee's prefix bonus of 12). A real `zz/workshop` scores 52 in its own name, and frizbee reports the first best alignment, so it gets no name bonus. fff returns 4,000 of them (files newest first, folders in path order). `through_ties` sees the tie run past those and keeps 2,000; in the window's Any Kind search files and folders take turns, so about half of each. The strict check then reads the path inside the folder, drops everything that matched only through `work/`, and lists what is left: the real matches that happened to be among the newest files or first folders. If none is, and Allow typos is on, the near-miss fallback finds nothing either: No Results, "The search looked only in work", and no `+`.

Files with the word in their own name are rescued by fff-search's filename pass only while the folder has at most 15,000 files. Folders, and files matched through an inner folder's name, never are.

What should happen: every item whose path inside the folder has the word is listed. The manual sentence added by 5624239 says "A search of only one folder looks in the path inside the folder searched, so the folder's own name doesn't count".

How new it is: plainly named folders behaved this way on upstream too. Folders with a space or one of `*?[]{}!\` in their path were fetched 20,000 wide until 5ebf1cf removed that, so for them (`My Documents`, `Google Drive`, `OneDrive - Contoso`) this is a regression between about 4,000 and 20,000 items. It is the recorded "cut before the strict check" limit, but here it holds for every item of the folder and for correctly spelled words.

Not run: the scores and thresholds are read from the fff-search and neo_frizbee sources.
findings.code_path: crates/fffinder-core/src/engine.rs:1061-1069 (the folder goes to fff as Constraint::Glob only) -> :1092-1099 (`fetch` is (limit*4).max(2_000) unless wide or one letter; the folder over-fetch was dropped in 5ebf1cf) -> :1135-1137, :1157-1179, :1208-1210 (fff search, then `through_ties`) -> :2647-2661 (`through_ties` falls back to `fetch` when the tie runs past what fff returned) -> :2685-2712 (`best_of_both` takes a file and a folder in turn on equal scores) -> :1226-1234 (`rel` is the path inside the searched folder) -> :990-1002 (strict check and near-miss fallback read `rel`). fff-search-0.11.0/src/score.rs:54-90 (words matched on the whole relative path), :482-497 (a folder gets its name bonus only when the match starts in its last segment), :661 (filename pass off above 15,000 path matches), :734. neo_frizbee-0.13.3/src/const.rs:6-7 (prefix 12, delimiter 4); src/smith_waterman/algo/mod.rs:196 (`>` keeps the first best alignment).
findings.tests_gap: Every test that searches a folder for a word in its own name uses a folder of two or three files (engine.rs:4348 `catalog` in Catalog, 4486-4553 `invoice` in invoices), where the whole folder is in the pool. The crowding tests (engine.rs:6114 name search, 6059 content search) put the better matches outside the folder, which the glob now keeps out. No test has more items inside the searched folder than the pool keeps while the word is in the folder's own path.
findings.fix: In `search_root`, fetch wide (`limit.max(20_000)`, as for a one-letter or quoted search) when a folder inside the root is searched and every fuzzy word of two bytes or more has its letters in order in the folder's own path inside the location (the lowercased `scope.strip_prefix(&base)`). Those are exactly the searches whose pool fff fills with matches the check discards. That covers folders up to about 20,000 items. A complete fix would page on with `PaginationArgs.offset` while the strict check leaves fewer than `limit` hits and `total_matched` exceeds what was fetched.

Search { query: "work", scope: root/work, files_only: true, limit: 10 } and expect ["ci.yml"]. By reading, today it returns nothing: the 4,000 newest tie, 2,000 are kept, and none has w-o-r-k inside the folder. A second case: 4,100 folders `work/d-NNNN` plus `work/zz/workshop`, Kind Folder, expecting ["workshop"].

findings.title: After a date sort falls back at its read bound, the answer says no sort chooses, so a later Size, Name or Kind sort only reorders the best-ranked rows
findings.scenario:
Steps: Results shown 5,000, or any Nushell filter on (the search limit is then 5,000). A name search with more than 5,000 names matching, such as `*.log` or a common word; the status bar shows `+`. Choose Sort By Date Created (or the Date Last Opened header), then Sort By Size.

What happens: for the date sort the engine reads only the `limit.max(5_000)` best-ranked hits from the disk. With a limit of 5,000 those all fit, so `cut_in_order` returns None and the engine answers with the unsorted list and `sort_chooses: false`. That part is documented. The window keeps the flag and reads it as "no sort would choose". On the Size click `result_sort_changed` only calls `read_more_for_results`, no search runs, and the rows are the largest of the 5,000 best-ranked. Going from Relevance straight to Size does search again and lists the largest 5,000 of up to 20,000 matches per location. The same search under the same sort therefore lists different items depending on which sort was clicked before, until the next keystroke or Refresh.

What should happen: the manual says of a list with a `+`: "sorting it by anything else searches again and lists the first of every match in that order". A fallback that is specific to the sort key should not switch that off for other keys.
findings.code_path: crates/fffinder-core/src/engine.rs:2157-2165 (`sort_before_cut` keeps `limit.max(SORT_READS)` hits that need a disk read) -> :2076-2082 (`cut_in_order`: set aside and not truncated gives None) -> :1017-1023 (`sort_chooses: false, ..unsorted`) -> src/finder/mod.rs:2253-2254 (kept in SearchStats) -> src/finder/mod.rs:2347-2357 (`result_sort_changed`: `!stats.sort_chooses` leads only to `read_more_for_results`) -> src/finder/list.rs:115-121. The limit of 5,000 comes from src/finder/mod.rs:2198-2202 (`FILTER_SEARCH_LIMIT.max(result_limit)`).
findings.tests_gap: engine::tests::a_sort_by_a_date_on_the_disk_reads_only_the_best_hits and the controls tests check one sort at a time. Nothing changes the sort key after a fallback, and no window test runs with a limit of 5,000 and more than 5,000 matches under a date sort.
findings.fix: Tell the two reasons for None apart. Keep `sort_chooses: false` when the names with the words fit (`sort_before_cut` returned false, or nothing was dropped by the read bound). When the read bound is what left too few, return the unsorted list with `sort_chooses: true`, so the window searches again on the next sort change. Alternatively the window could remember which key the answer was made under and search again when the key changes away from one that reads the disk.
findings.test_idea: Engine test: 5,010 files `note-NNNN.txt` with distinct sizes. Search { query: "note", limit: 5000, files_only: true, sort: Created descending } and assert the answer still says a sort may choose; today `sort_chooses` is false. Then the same request with Size descending must hold the largest file, which the unsorted 5,000 need not. Or a controls test with Results shown 5,000: click Date Created, then Size, and expect a search in flight after the second click.

findings.title: For a search of one folder, `changes_for` looks for the words from the search location down, so files the search cannot list keep running it again and it falls minutes behind
findings.scenario:
Steps: search location /home/me; Search Only in "Documents"; type `docu` (or `atlas` inside Projects/atlas). Another program creates /home/me/Documents/Tax Return.pdf.

What happens: `Changes::note` stores each new file's path inside the index's folder, `documents/tax return.pdf`, and `changes_for` checks the words against that string for a folder search too. It has d-o-c-u, so the file is reported as the search's business. `Engine::search` checks the path inside the searched folder, `tax return.pdf`, and cannot list it. The window runs the search again quietly, the answer is unchanged, and `Behind::caught_up(false)` counts a miss. With files arriving regularly in that folder, every one of them is "news", and the reruns back off to one in 127 looks, about four minutes. A file that really matches is then listed minutes late, where it would show in about three seconds.

The same looseness holds for a one-letter search: `Engine::search` wants the letter in the name, `changes_for` accepts it anywhere in the path.

What should happen: `changes_for` should judge a new file by the text the search checks, as the comment at engine.rs:426-428 already intends for the index's own path.

Apart from this, `strict_words` and the words `Engine::search` checks agreed in a Python port run over 5.4 million generated queries, and `changes_for` is a superset of what a search lists except for near misses, which the manual states.
findings.code_path: crates/fffinder-core/src/engine.rs:425-431 (`note`: `lower` is the path inside the index's base) -> :747-755 (`changes_for`: `scope` narrows by prefix only, and `words.iter().all(|word| is_subsequence(word, lower))` reads the base-relative path) against :1226-1234 and :990 (`Engine::search` checks `hit.rel`, the path inside the searched folder) and :1119-1124 (a one-letter search checks the name). Pacing: src/finder/mod.rs:1635-1646 (`news`, `fell_behind`), :429-453 (`due`, `caught_up`: wait = 2^misses - 1 looks).
findings.tests_gap: engine::tests::a_search_is_told_which_changes_are_its_business asserts the folder cases only with `tax`, which is in the file's name (engine.rs:3648-3653). what_a_search_lists_is_among_the_changes_that_matter_to_it checks one direction only: everything listed must matter. Nothing asserts that a file a folder search cannot list is left out.
findings.fix: In `changes_for`, when `scope` is kept (it is spelled like the paths), look for the words in `path.strip_prefix(scope)` lowercased in place of `lower`. For a search whose only word is one letter, look in the file's name.
findings.test_idea: Add to a_search_is_told_which_changes_are_its_business: `told(&SearchRequest { scope: Some("/home/me/Documents".into()), ..search("docu") })` should be `paths(&[])`. Today it is `paths(&[new])`. The engine already pins the other side: `invoice` searched inside `invoices` lists nothing (engine.rs:4544-4548).

findings.title: Results of a folder search outside the search locations silently stop following changes once three other such folders have been searched
findings.scenario:
Steps: tab 1 runs Search Only in a folder F1 outside every search location, by name, and leaves its results showing. In another tab or window, search three more outside folders F2, F3 and F4 one after the other. Then create or remove a matching file in F1.

What happens: `indexes_for` keeps the three most recently created temporary indexes. Finding an existing one does not move it to the front, so creating F4's index drops F1's even while F1's results are on screen. fff-search's watcher threads hold only weak handles, so the index, its watcher and the callback into `Changes` go with it. F1's folder stays in `log.bases`, so `changes_for` still narrows by the scope and answers `Some(vec![])` for everything else. The window never has news for tab 1, and its list stays as it was until the user types or presses Refresh. That keystroke rebuilds F1's index from scratch and evicts another tab's.

What should happen: the manual says a search by name "runs again by itself a few seconds after a file it lists, or could list, comes or goes" and that folders outside the search locations get a temporary index. Nothing says such a search can stop following.

The cap and the eviction order are upstream's; the stale list is new with live results. Not run: the mechanism is read from the engine and from fff-search's weak handles.
findings.code_path: crates/fffinder-core/src/engine.rs:28 (MAX_ADHOC = 3) -> :851-853 (an existing index is returned without being moved) -> :857-861 (insert at the front, truncate) -> the dropped RootIndex was the last strong SharedFilePicker (fff-search-0.11.0/src/watcher/background_watcher.rs:93 and :194 hold weak handles; src/watcher/watch.rs:566-570 shuts the registry down on drop) -> engine.rs:457-462 (`reports` never forgets a base) -> :747-755 (the scope still narrows, so `Some(vec![])`) -> src/finder/mod.rs:1611-1646 (no news, no rerun).
findings.tests_gap: The live-results tests use search locations only. `report_change_for_test` expects "a file in a search location" (engine.rs:798), so a temporary index cannot be staged, and the record's left_out covers temporary indexes only before their watcher is up.
findings.fix: In `indexes_for`, move a temporary index that is found to the front of `adhoc`, so the one evicted is the least recently searched and not the oldest made. That still leaves a fourth concurrent folder unfollowed; raising MAX_ADHOC or having `changes_for` say so when the scope's index is gone are the next steps, and the second needs care not to make evicted tabs rebuild each other's indexes in turn.
findings.test_idea: Engine test with `watch: true`: search four folders outside the roots in turn (after `prepare`), then search the first again and assert no new scan was started for it, for instance `indexing == false` on the answer at once. Today the first folder's index is gone and is rebuilt. A window test would write a file into the first folder after the fourth search and wait for it to be listed.

On the proposed fixes:

- The engine-side change in root_spelling covers all of those: canonicalize always, and return the root-spelled path when it differs. The recursion ends, because the second call gets the path it would return.
- One case stays open with the engine-side change: a symlink inside a search location that points outside every location. root_spelling finds no location for the real path, and indexes_for (engine.rs:842-850) still picks the location by text, so the glob is `link/**` and nothing is found. indexes_for would have to judge by the real path too.
